examples.text: The baby is asleep at last.
Kim fell asleep on the sofa in front of the television.
Is he still asleep? It's almost noon.
I was so tired that I was asleep before my head touched the pillow.

compare.note: sleep is the verb for the activity: she slept for an hour; asleep names the state: she was asleep
sleepy means wanting to sleep, not sleeping

adaptation.semantic: Most languages express this state with a verb: she sleeps, she is sleeping. English uses be plus asleep for the state and the verb sleep for the activity, so a translation may need a verb where English has an adjective.

senses.definition: (of an arm, leg, hand, or foot) without feeling for a short time, usually because you have been sitting or lying on it

examples.text: My foot is asleep from sitting on it.
I couldn't stand up right away because my leg was asleep.
Her arm was asleep because she had been lying on it.

synonyms.note: numb is the general word and is also used for cold

adaptation.semantic: Many languages say that a limb has gone to sleep or is numb; the English adjective asleep is used of the limb itself, with be or go: my foot is asleep, my foot went to sleep.

phrases.definition: sleeping very deeply, so that it is hard to wake you
phrases.explanation: Sound asleep means the same. Fast here has an old meaning, firmly, that survives in almost no other phrase.

examples.text: The children were fast asleep by nine.
He was fast asleep and did not hear the phone.

usage_note: To say that someone begins to sleep, use fall asleep or go to sleep. Asleep itself never comes before a noun: a sleeping child, not an asleep child.

learner_errors.note: Asleep is used only after a verb such as be; before a noun use sleeping.

learner_errors.incorrect: I went asleep during the movie.
learner_errors.correct: I fell asleep during the movie.
learner_errors.note: The verb that goes with asleep is fall. Go to sleep is also possible, but not go asleep.

etymology.text: Asleep was formed from an old short form of on or in plus sleep, so at first it meant in sleep. That is why it acts like a phrase after a verb and never comes before a noun; awake, alive, and alone were formed in the same way.

adaptation.grammar: Asleep is used only after a verb such as be, fall, or lie, never before a noun; the same is true of awake, alive, alone, and afraid. It has no comparative form; degree is shown with fast, sound, or half: half asleep.
adaptation.pronunciation: The stress is on the second syllable, and the first vowel is the weak sound ə, as in about.
